components: say (言) with a stroke in the mouth
etymology: Derived from 言 'say' by adding a stroke inside the mouth — sound held in the mouth: tone without words yet.
mnemonic: A voice standing (立) on the sun (日), humming with no words — おと. Pure sound, waiting to become speech: turn up the 音楽.

etymology: Pictograph: a dog — the oracle-bone form shows the whole animal; the modern form keeps a big body (大) and one dot for the ear.
mnemonic: A big (大) creature with one flea (the dot) it can't stop scratching — いぬ. Man's best friend, one stroke away from 'big'.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a child (子) raised under a roof (宀). Characters were the 'children' bred in the house of writing — simple signs combined and multiplied.
mnemonic: A child under the roof of the schoolhouse, copying its very first letter — ジ. Kanji breed like children: two simple ones move in together and a new 字 is born.

etymology: Compound ideograph: three trees (木) — more trees than a grove (林): a forest.
mnemonic: One tree is a tree, two is a grove (林), three is a forest deep enough to get lost in — もり. Count the canopy: the third tree sits on top of the other two.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a foot (止) marching straight at a line/target (一) — going straight at it: correct, upright.
mnemonic: Walk the straight line without wobbling: that is correct — ただしい. Teachers count scores with this kanji, one stroke per point: five strokes, one 正.

etymology: Compound: a sprout (生, worn down) over a well or mineral vein (丹→月) — the fresh blue-green of plants over deep water. Japanese 青 spans both blue and green.
mnemonic: Young shoots reflected in a well: that fresh color between green and blue — あおい. Traffic lights in Japan turn 青 — blue — even when they look green.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a person (大) beside a great fire (火, flattened at the bottom) — skin glowing red in the blaze.
mnemonic: Stand big and close to the bonfire and your face turns red — あかい. A newborn is a 赤ちゃん: red-faced and yelling.

etymology: Compound: the sun (日) just clearing the top of a pole (十) — the first hour of daylight: early.
mnemonic: The sun climbing the flagpole at dawn while everyone sleeps — はやい. Early and fast are the same kanji: the sun wastes no time.

etymology: Originally written 邨 (with a phonetic); the modern form is wood (木) + hand-measure (寸) — a settlement measured out in timber.
mnemonic: A hand (寸) pacing out plots between the trees (木): here the well, there the houses — a village, むら. Every RPG starts in one.

etymology: Phono-semantic: rice field (田) + 丁 (phonetic チョウ) — the raised paths dividing fields into neat blocks; then the blocks of a town.
mnemonic: Fields (田) nailed (丁) into a tidy grid of streets — まち. The address system still counts in 丁目: block one, block two.

etymology: Pictograph: a rice paddy seen from above — the box is the dike, the cross the footpaths between plots.
mnemonic: A perfect aerial photo of a paddy: four plots, two paths — た. It grows inside half the surnames of Japan: 田中, 山田, 本田.

etymology: Pictograph: a standing figure with a pattern tattooed on the chest — ornament, pattern, and from there writing and literature.
mnemonic: A scholar in a crossed robe, patterns inked on his chest: the first text was worn, not written — ブン. 文学 is that ink grown into literature.

etymology: Pictograph: the crescent moon just risen — half of 月, for the half-lit hour of dusk.
mnemonic: The moon with one stroke still missing: too early for full night — ゆう, the evening. 夕方 is when the sky can't decide.

etymology: Pictograph: a flexed arm with its bulge of muscle — or, by another old reading, a plow biting the earth. Raw strength either way.
mnemonic: A bicep curling into a hook — ちから. Wherever it hides in a kanji (男, 助, 動), someone is straining at something.

etymology: Compound ideograph: two trees (木) side by side — a stand of trees: a grove. Add a third and it thickens into 森.
mnemonic: Two trees planted like neighbors, close enough to share shade — はやし. Halfway between one lonely 木 and the deep 森.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a bow (弓) plus a single vertical stroke — the string drawn back: to pull.
mnemonic: Grab the bowstring (the lone stroke) and pull the bow (弓) to full stretch — ひく. Doors in Japan tell you which side does it: 引 pull, 押 push.

etymology: Phono-semantic: movement (辶) + 袁 'long flowing robe' (phonetic エン) — a walk so long you need your traveling robe: distant.
mnemonic: Hitch up the long robe and start walking: it's far — とおい. 遠足 is the school excursion that never seems to end.

etymology: Pictograph: a grand masked dancer — a great head with trailing legs (夂) — from the midsummer festival dances of ancient China.
mnemonic: A masked dancer stamping slow steps in the heat of the festival night — なつ. Summer is when the mask comes out and the legs drag.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a pig (豕) under a roof (宀) — livestock beneath the family roof was the ancient household's wealth: home.
mnemonic: A pig snoring under the roof: the house is doing well — いえ. Home is where the bacon sleeps; the ~カ ending also names the expert 'of the house': 作家, 画家.

etymology: Phono-semantic: 哥 (two 可, phonetic カ) + 欠, the wide-open mouth — breath pouring out in melody: song.
mnemonic: Two karaoke prompts (可可) and a mouth thrown wide open (欠) — うた! The 歌手 holds the note; you hold the remote.

etymology: Simplified from 畫: a hand with a brush (聿) drawing the boundaries of a field (田) — to draw; a drawn stroke; a picture.
mnemonic: A framed field hung on the wall: the first landscape painting — ガ. Movies are 映画, moving pictures; each kanji stroke is one 画.

etymology: Pictograph: a spiral, squared by the brush into a box within a box — turning around, a revolution, hence a counter for repetitions.
mnemonic: A whirlpool drawn with a ruler: around and around — まわる. Each full loop counts one time: 一回, 二回, 三回.

etymology: Phono-semantic: water (氵) + 毎 'every' (phonetic カイ) — the water every river runs home to: the sea.
mnemonic: Every (毎) drop of water (氵) ends up in the same place — うみ. Mother ocean: look closely, 母 is sitting inside 毎.

etymology: Simplified from 樂: a great drum hung with bells on a wooden stand (木) — music; and the ease and pleasure music brings.
mnemonic: A festival drum on its wooden stand, bells jingling on both sides — music, ガク; and the crowd's face: 楽しい, たのしい. One kanji, both the song and the smile.

etymology: Phono-semantic: 彦 'handsome young man' (phonetic ガン) + 頁 'head' — the front of the head at its most presentable: the face.
mnemonic: The handsome one (彦) turns his head (頁) toward the camera: that's the face — かお. 顔 is what 洗顔 washes and 笑顔 lights up.

etymology: Simplified from 歸: troops (𠂤) coming back to the wife's broom (帚) — the soldier returning to swept floors: to go home.
mnemonic: The sword hung up at the door, the broom waiting inside: homecoming — かえる. ただいま! is this kanji spoken aloud.

etymology: Pictograph: an ox head seen from the front — the top strokes are the horns, the vertical its long face.
mnemonic: Face-to-face with an ox: one horn up, ears out, the long nose down the middle — うし. 牛乳 is what it gives; 牛肉 is what it becomes.

etymology: Pictograph: a tall building raised on high ground — the watchtower of the royal city: the capital.
mnemonic: A palace tower on the hill, visible for miles: you've reached the capital — キョウ. It anchors both 東京 and 京都 — the new capital and the old.

etymology: Originally the name of a hard-shelled weevil; borrowed early for 彊 'powerful bow'. The bow (弓) stayed on as the character's anchor of meaning.
mnemonic: A bow (弓) so taut even the armored beetle (虫) bounces off — つよい. 勉強, studying, is this strength applied to your own skull.

etymology: Compound: a child (子) under crossed counting-sticks (爻), with the master's hand holding a rod (攵) — instruction, old style: to teach.
mnemonic: The old master taps the board, the child copies the crossed strokes — おしえる. 教室 is the room where the tapping happens.

etymology: Phono-semantic: movement (辶) + 斤 'axe' (phonetic キン) — within walking distance of the sound of the axe: near.
mnemonic: If you can hear the axe chopping, you're almost there — ちかい. 近所 is everything within one axe-echo of your door.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a mouth (口) on legs (儿) — the sibling old enough to speak for the others: the elder brother.
mnemonic: A walking mouth that never stops giving orders — あに. Politely he's お兄さん; in the kanji he's still just a bossy mouth on legs.

etymology: Compound ideograph: words (言) + ten (十) — counting out loud to ten: to reckon, measure, plan.
mnemonic: Count to ten before you act — that's a plan, ケイ. The 時計 on your wrist counts for you, all day long.

etymology: Pictograph: a person (儿) with the head emphasized by two strokes — the head as the origin-point of the body: beginning, source.
mnemonic: A pair of legs carrying the 'first thing' on top: the head, where everything starts — もと. 元気 is your original energy, factory settings restored.

etymology: Compound ideograph: fire (火, flattened) carried on a person's legs (儿) — a torch-bearer: light on the move, rays.
mnemonic: A runner carrying the torch through the dark, sparks streaming — ひかり. Light with legs: that's a ray.

etymology: Pictograph: a carpenter's square or work-tool — craft, work, construction. One of the oldest tool-signs in the script.
mnemonic: An I-beam standing in the frame of a building site — コウ. Wherever 工 appears (工事, 工場), someone in a helmet is measuring twice.

etymology: Simplified from 廣: a building (广) with a vast interior (the phonetic 黄 reduced to 厶) — a roomy hall: wide, spacious.
mnemonic: Under one roof, so much empty floor that a single elbow (厶) rattles around in it — ひろい. 広場: the wide-open plaza.

etymology: Phono-semantic: an old man (耂) + a bent breath-stroke (丂, phonetic コウ) — the elder bent over a question: to ponder.
mnemonic: The old master strokes his beard, thoughts bending like the bottom stroke — かんがえる. Real thinking has a crook in it.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a lid (亼) settling onto a mouth or vessel (口) — two halves made for each other: to fit, to match.
mnemonic: The lid clicks perfectly onto the jar — あう. Whatever matches, matches here: 試合 a match of players, 都合 a match of schedules.

etymology: Simplified from 黑: a chimney vent blackened by the fire (灬) burning below — soot: black.
mnemonic: Look up the chimney over the flames: everything the smoke touched is black — くろい. The four dots are the fire still cooking the soot.

etymology: Phono-semantic: person (亻) + 乍 'to hew, notch' (phonetic サク) — a person cutting something into shape: to make.
mnemonic: A craftsman notching wood, chip by chip, until the thing exists — つくる. The 作家 hews sentences instead.

etymology: Phono-semantic: woman (女) + a right side descended from an old phonetic (written like 市 'market' today) — the elder sister.
mnemonic: The young woman (女) sent to the market (市) with the family purse: responsibility means you're the elder sister — あね, お姉さん.

etymology: Pictograph: a pole with a banner (亠) raised over cloth stalls (巾) — the sign that market day is on; later the market town, the city.
mnemonic: Raise the flag over the cloth stalls and the whole town gathers — いち, the market; シ, the city it grew into (広島市, 京都市).

etymology: Compound ideograph: originally the fontanelle/brain (囟, later confused with 田) over the heart (心) — brain and heart working together: to think, to feel.
mnemonic: The field on top is your brain's little plot; the heart below waters it — おもう. In Japanese you think with both: と思います.

etymology: Pictograph: a footprint — the foot planted: to stop. As a component it walks through 歩, 正, 歴 and dozens more.
mnemonic: A foot slammed flat on the ground: halt! — とまる. Red sign in Japan: 止まれ. The footprint that refuses to move.

etymology: Phono-semantic: thread (糸) + 氏 (phonetic シ) — sheets felted from silk and plant fiber: paper, which China invented from exactly that.
mnemonic: Mash the fibers (糸) flat and let them dry into a sheet — かみ. A 手紙 is fiber that carries your handwriting across the country.

etymology: Pictograph: a nose seen from the front. To this day Japanese speakers point at their nose to say 'me?' — oneself.
mnemonic: Point at your own nose: me, myself — ジ. Everything automatic (自動), self-made (自分) or free-willed (自由) starts at the nose.
